title: chore: update every dependency to its latest release
body:
`cargo update` across the whole graph, plus the manifest bumps needed to cross a major boundary.

| Crate | From | To |
|---|---|---|
| `vta-sdk` | 0.20.24 | 0.21.7 |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` | 0.18.60 | 0.19.2 |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.2 | 0.3.0 |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.1 | 0.2.0 |
| `vta-service` (dev) | 0.13 | 0.14.16 |
| `affinidi-messaging-core` (floor) | 0.1.5 | 0.1.6 |

## The one source change

`affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.6 marks `Protocol` `#[non_exhaustive]` and adds a
`DIDCommV1` variant (Aries RFC 0019), so the inbound dispatcher's `match` in
`openvtc-core/src/didcomm.rs` no longer compiles as written.

It gains a wildcard arm that logs and drops. That is the correct handling, not a
placeholder: OpenVTC speaks DIDComm v2.1 and TSP, neither listener it installs
ever negotiates v1, and nothing downstream of that match could read a v1
payload. The arm is also what keeps the *next* variant from being a compile
break.

The core floor moves to 0.1.6 to match. This is load-bearing rather than
cosmetic — on 0.1.5 the enum has neither the attribute nor the variant, so the
wildcard is an unreachable pattern and `-D warnings` rejects it. I checked
0.1.4/0.1.5/0.1.6 sources directly rather than assuming.

Everything else rode the bump untouched — the join ceremony, the reciprocal VMC
exchange, and the TSP leg all dispatch on `vta_sdk::protocols` constants rather
than string literals. That indirection is why this is mostly a lockfile change
and not an audit of every dispatch site.

## `deny.toml`: two ignores removed

RUSTSEC-2026-0215 (`smallstr` unmaintained) and RUSTSEC-2024-0370
(`proc-macro-error` unmaintained). Both crates left the graph with this refresh —
verified against the lockfile, not just inferred from `cargo deny`'s
unmatched-ignore warning — exactly as each ignore's comment predicted. The
remaining ignores still match and stay.

## Pins that survive re-evaluation

`rand` 0.8 and `x25519-dalek` 2.x stay. `pgp` 0.20.0 is still the latest release
and its manifest still declares `rand ^0.8.6` / `x25519-dalek ^2.0.1`; I read the
published manifest rather than trusting the existing comment. Comment date
refreshed to record the re-check.

`generic-array` and `matchit` remain behind latest — both transitively pinned by
other crates, not reachable from our manifests.

## Known duplicate, upstream to fix

`did-git-sign` 0.4.1 still depends on `vta-sdk` 0.19.28, so the binary links two
vta-sdk majors. That belongs to `verifiable-git-infrastructure`, not here — per
CLAUDE.md, protocol/infra changes target that repo. Recorded in the CHANGELOG so
it is not silently carried.

## Verified

- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo deny check` — advisories, bans, licenses, sources all ok
- `cargo test --workspace --all-features` — **640 passed, 0 failed**
- `cargo test --workspace --all-features -- --ignored` — **13 passed, 0 failed**.
  These are the ones that actually exercise the bumped crates: the in-process
  mediator transport round-trip, the join/self-remove lifecycle, and the MockVta
  bootstrap against `vta-service` 0.14.
- Builds check under default, `--all-features`, and `--no-default-features`.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers
```

Checklist note, honestly: this PR adds no outbound client, no retry loop, no lock
scope and no mutation — the only source change is a drop arm in an existing
inbound dispatch loop, which is a `continue` in a loop that already survived
unparseable frames the same way. The boxes are ticked as "unchanged and still
true", not as new work verified.

title: chore(deps): hard-pin the enforced-authcrypt TDK and refresh the lockfile
body:
Supersedes #900.

## Why #900 could not be rebased

#900 was authored on 6 Aug against a main that has since moved. **#902 already
landed the substance of it**: the direct `affinidi-messaging-sdk` pins in
`vta-sdk` / `vta-service` / `tests/e2e` are on `0.19`, and the
`UnpackMetadata` `#[non_exhaustive]` test helper in `vti-common` is fixed
(with a better comment than #900 carried). Rebasing #900 would resolve to a
diff of one manifest line plus a stale lockfile, and its three version bumps
(`vti-common` 0.11.35, `vta-sdk` 0.21.7, `vta-service` 0.14.11) are all
already claimed on main by other PRs. Its changelog fragment filename also
collides with `changelog.d/900-envelope-type-from-the-binding-crate.md`.

This PR carries forward what was genuinely left, and finishes the job.

## The pin

`affinidi-tdk = "0.8"` accepted any 0.8.x. The enforced-authcrypt fix
(affinidi-tdk-rs #671) — `unpack` rejecting plaintext / anoncrypt /
forged-`from` envelopes **by default** — first ships in **0.8.5**, through
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19 + `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` 0.15.8.

The lockfile happened to hold 0.8.5, so the property held *by accident*. A
`cargo update`, a lockfile regeneration, or a clean checkout resolving afresh
could each move sender authentication back out of the library, and nothing
would flag it. The requirement now states what the code depends on, with the
reason recorded at the pin.

Defence in depth is unchanged: `bind_authcrypt_sender` and the DIDComm
`inbound_gate` still enforce this above the library.

## A dead workspace dependency

`affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` is removed from
`[workspace.dependencies]`. No member consumes it — it is absent from
`Cargo.lock` entirely, and `vta-service` and `vtc-service` both carry comments
recording that they replaced it with local `shim.rs` / `router.rs`
equivalents. #900 proposed bumping it to `0.3.22`; that would have been inert.
A requirement that resolves nothing is worse than no requirement, because it
reads as a supported edge.

## Lockfile refresh

`cargo update` collapses two long-standing duplicate trees:

- **`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.18.65 is gone.** It survived behind
  `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` → `affinidi-messaging-mediator` — the
  dev-only e2e / `vtc-service` fixture chain #902 explicitly called out as
  still carrying a 0.18 copy. `test-mediator` 0.2.47 moved to sdk 0.19, and
  `mediator` 0.18.9 with it. The graph now holds **one** messaging SDK.
- **The legacy `ssi-*` stack drops out** — `ssi-jwk`, `ssi-jws`,
  `ssi-dids-core`, `ssi-json-ld` and ~15 siblings — taking `reqwest` 0.11,
  `sha2` 0.9, `ripemd160`, `tiny-keccak`, `uint` and `windows-sys` 0.48 with
  it. `reqwest` unifies on 0.13.4.

Net **−1393** lockfile lines.

`curve25519-dalek` (5) and `ed25519-dalek` (3) stay single, as #887 / #889 /
#890 left them. `elliptic-curve`, `ecdsa`, `p256` and `sha2` remain doubled
across the RustCrypto 0.13 → 0.14 transition — still upstream-gated, not
something this PR can close.

## Scope

Manifest + lockfile only. No workspace crate's source changes, so no version
bumps and nothing to publish.

## Verified

- `cargo check --workspace --locked` on 1.97
- `cargo check --workspace --locked` on **MSRV 1.95.0**
- `cargo clippy --workspace --locked -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --locked`
- `scripts/check-lockfile-self-pins.sh` — no workspace crate pulled from crates.io

title: DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its taskContext binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)
body:
# DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its `taskContext` binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)

## Context

[trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/11) flagged that DTG Core Credentials placed normative requirements on `taskContext`-bearing credentials (outcome evidence, terminal states, etc.) that depended on "the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification" — which doesn't exist yet, so the requirements were untestable.

Resolution ([dtgwg-cred-spec#15](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/15)) restructures that section to depend only on mechanisms **already defined in this framework's current editor's draft**, rather than on any future spec:

- **Terminal state** = presence of a `#response`-variant document ([§4.4.1](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#441-request-and-response-variants)) or a `trust-task-error` document ([§8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#8-error-responses)), correlated by `threadId` ([§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member)).
- **Outcome integrity** = the existing per-specification `proof`-required declaration ([§7.3 item 8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Outcome artifact structure** = the existing per-specification `#response` payload schema ([§7.3 item 7.6](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Evidence discovery / retrieval authorization / confidentiality** — sidestepped for cred-spec's v1.0 by requiring the outcome document to travel *with* the credential presentation, rather than be discovered/retrieved asynchronously by a verifier who wasn't party to the original exchange. (This framework's bilateral, transport-bound request/response model doesn't naturally support that kind of later, third-party retrieval, so cred-spec isn't relying on it.)

cred-spec now requires that any Trust Task specification a VTC/VTN designates as the referent of a DTG credential's `taskContext` — a "qualifying" specification — declare `proof` REQUIRED on its response/error variants and define a `#response` schema (or rely on `trust-task-error`). That's it; no framework behavior change required for this to work.

**No action needed on your side for cred-spec's fix to land.** Filing this mainly so you're aware of the cross-reference (per the coordination cred-spec's Governance Considerations already calls for between the two task forces), and to flag one small, genuinely optional framework enhancement that would make part of this more robust.

## Optional ask: let a Trust Task specification declare `threadId` as REQUIRED-and-unique

cred-spec needs `taskContext` (its own name for a `threadId`) to reliably name *one specific* exchange. Right now `threadId` is framework-wide `MAY`, and [§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member) is explicit that it "carries no normative validation semantics" — no presence guarantee, no uniqueness guarantee, and consumers can't reject on it.

cred-spec works around this by putting the uniqueness burden entirely on DTG *issuers* (its own conformance target), which is sufficient for cred-spec's purposes but means the framework's own consumer-side machinery can't enforce it — a misbehaving issuer's threadId reuse isn't independently rejectable the way, say, a missing required `proof` is (`proofRequired`, [§7.2 item 7](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

Proposal: add a declarable property to [§7.3](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements), mirroring item 8's Proof requirement pattern:

> **Thread requirement** — an explicit statement of whether `threadId` is OPTIONAL or REQUIRED for documents implementing the specification, together (where REQUIRED) with the uniqueness scope it MUST satisfy (e.g., "unique per exchange instance for the life of the specification's use"). A conforming consumer MUST reject a document lacking a REQUIRED `threadId` with `malformedRequest`, consistent with the existing `recipient`-required pattern ([§7.2 item 5](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

This is additive only — it doesn't touch `threadId`'s existing general-purpose, loosely-specified behavior for specifications that don't opt in. It would let a future DTG-ceremony Trust Task specification (or any other specification with the same need) get framework-level enforcement instead of relying on the depending spec's issuer-side discipline alone.

Happy to draft this as a PR here if it's wanted, or to help co-author a worked-example Trust Task specification for a DTG ceremony (e.g. relationship witnessing) satisfying the "qualifying" profile above, as a joint appendix in either repo — similar in spirit to your own Appendix A. Let us know which is useful.

title: feat(bindings): draft the DIDComm v1 binding specification
body:
`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` shipped in #187 without a binding specification to
implement, leaving the carriage and identity rules stated only in Rust doc
comments. This writes them down.

Written **from** the working implementation rather than ahead of it, so the open
questions are concrete, and structured to mirror `bindings/didcomm/0.2` section
for section — a reader who knows the v2.1 binding can diff them.

## What v1 forces that v2.1 did not

**No envelope type of its own.** It rides Aries `basic-message`, whose type has
two interchangeable document URIs. Credo emits the `https://didcomm.org` one by
default, so §1 requires consumers to treat them as equivalent and **forbids**
comparing `@type` by string equality — which silently drops conforming peers.

**Carriage had to be chosen.** v2.1 puts the document in `body`; v1 has none, and
RFC 0095 types `content` as a display string. §2 specifies an `~attach` decorator
under the reserved id `trust-task`; §2.1 records the alternatives and why not.

**Attribution takes a step more, normatively.** A v2.1 envelope authenticates a
DID. A v1 envelope carries **no DID at all** — a bare verkey, with the
verkey→DID binding held as connection state. §3 enumerates three outcomes rather
than two, and requires consumers to distinguish *"nobody authenticated this"*
from *"somebody did and we cannot name them"*. The second is a missing connection
record on the receiving side; collapsing them hides an operational fault behind
what looks like a hostile message.

**Threading needs the wire value, not the defaulted one.** §3.1 maps `thid`/`pthid`
per SPEC §9.1 and requires comparison against the `thid` *as it appeared on the
wire*. RFC 0008 defaults an absent `thid` to the message `@id`, a different
identifier space from the document's `id`, so comparing the defaulted value
manufactures disagreements out of conforming messages.

## Open questions are marked as such

§2 carries an explicit ⚠ flag — including whether `basic-message` is the right
carrier at all. Its assumed advantage is reach, but a consumer needs a handler
under *every* option considered, and v1 mediator forwarding is type-agnostic, so
a dedicated `@type` would route just as well and mirror `binding/didcomm/0.1`
more closely. Nothing depends on the choice yet, so it stays cheap to change.

The Status section says plainly that this is a starting point for the DTG Core
Credentials task force to amend — useful to any reader, not just them, since it
marks what is settled and what isn't.

## Also

One row of the error mapping now matches what the crate actually does: anoncrypt
and unbound-verkey both yield `proofRequired` where the consumer has any means of
replying. I'd written the spec saying "no framework code applies" while the crate
mapped both to `proofRequired` — a contradiction worth catching before anyone
implemented against it.

Crate docs now cite the binding rather than describing it as forthcoming.

## Verification

Registry clean (288 specs, 405 example documents) · `cargo test --workspace` 31
suites · clippy clean · binding serves alongside the others
(`didcomm didcomm-v1 https push tsp`).

Refs #173

title: fix: don't wipe the generated tree on bad input, and make the receipt composable
body:
Two problems found while adding `vtc/relationships/request` in #190.

## 1. Codegen deleted before it validated

`clean_generated_tree` ran *before* the generate loop, so a spec that failed to
generate left the tree wiped. A malformed `payload.invalid-examples.json` — I
wrote `why` where the schema wants `note` — deleted **335 files**, left the
workspace uncompilable, and surfaced only as a later `cargo fmt` error about an
unresolvable `mod acl`, pointing nowhere near the file at fault.

`generate_one` no longer writes: it returns the path and contents, `main`
collects every module, and only once all have generated does the clean run and
the writes happen.

Verified by reintroducing the same bad input:

```
Error: failed to generate code for vtc/relationships/request/0.1
Caused by: …/payload.invalid-examples.json[0].note must be a string

modules before: 26      modules after: 26      outstanding diff: 0
```

title: feat(vtc): bring VRC request/issue onto Trust Tasks as relationships/request
body:
Finishes a migration that was already half done. `vtc/relationships/{publish,
list,graph,revoke}` exist; request/issue stayed on the legacy
`https://firstperson.network/vrc/1.0/*` DIDComm types. Promised to @bmiller59 on
#173.

## Three legacy message types → one specification

| legacy | becomes |
|---|---|
| `vrc/1.0/request` (`{reason?}`, 48h) | the request document |
| `vrc/1.0/issued` | its `#response`, carrying the signed `vrc` |
| `vrc/1.0/rejected` (`{reason?}`, by `thid`) | a `trust-task-error` with `vtc/relationships/request:declined` |

**Collapsing the rejection is the point of the migration, not a shortcut.** An
error response is already a Trust Task document — correlated by `threadId`,
validated and signed by the same pipeline, subject to §8.1's routing rules. A
bespoke `rejected` type means a second refusal path for every consumer to
implement and a second place to get that routing wrong. It also inherits §8.2's
`inResponseTo`, so a retained decline names the request it answers, which `thid`
correlation could never do for anyone outside the exchange.

The legacy protocol fixed the request's lifetime at 48 hours in code. That's the
envelope's `expiresAt` (§4.2) — a producer's choice with a consumer obligation to
honour it, rather than a constant baked into a message type.

## First real use of two 0.3 features

Neither contrived; both fit:

**Per-variant proof.** Request and response are REQUIRED for *different* reasons,
and the declaration now says so separately — an unsigned ask to mint a
relationship credential is a social-engineering surface, while the response
delivers a credential the requester retains and later publishes. Both land on
REQUIRED, but a reader can see which threat each addresses. This is the first
spec in the registry using the per-variant form.

**`targetFrameworkVersion: 0.3`** — joins `trust-task-error/0.3` as the only
specs validating against the envelope schema that recognises `parentThreadId`.

## Scope

`request` and `publish` stay separate exchanges, deliberately. `request` obtains
a VRC from its issuer; `publish` lodges one with the community so it appears in
`list` and `graph`. Neither implies the other — a VRC may be held privately, and
a member may publish one obtained by other means.

## Verification

Registry clean (287 specs, 402 example documents) · `cargo test --workspace` 31
suites · clippy clean · TS 43/43 · smoke passes · codegen idempotent both sides.

Generated constants confirm the per-variant declaration reaches the bindings on
both the request and response impls.

## One thing worth a follow-up

`trust-tasks-codegen` **deletes the generated tree before validating its inputs**.
A malformed `payload.invalid-examples.json` in this PR (I used `why` where the
schema wants `note`) left 335 files deleted and the workspace uncompilable, and
the only symptom was a downstream `cargo fmt` error about an unresolvable module
— nothing pointing at the actual file. `git checkout` recovers it, but validating
inputs before touching the tree would turn a confusing failure into a one-line
message. Not fixed here; happy to do it separately.

title: fix(consent): an approver need not hold VTA authority to answer
body:
## The bug

An approver device holds no authority to *act* — that is the entire point of the `approve_scope` axis — so it has no reason to hold an ACL entry. But the ACL check every intrinsic-sender transport runs before dispatch applied to `task-consent/decision` like any other task, and refused it.

That inverts the model. A decision is authorized by the **document**: the approver's Data-Integrity proof, checked against the policy-named approver set. `handle_decision` does not read its `AuthClaims` at all, and `policy_gate` already exempts ceremony tasks from re-gating. The surrounding consent code is explicitly built for an approver that may be absent from the ACL — `compute_delegated_contexts` and the gate's eligibility count both read "absent from the ACL" as *confers nothing*, never as *cannot speak*. Only the transport gate disagreed, and it disagreed first, before any of the code written to accommodate that approver could run.

Execution was never the issue: the grant is keyed to the requester and the task runs under the requester's claims. The approver's ACL entry was doing exactly one job — getting the message past the doorman.

## Why it was so hard to see

It failed silently in both directions. The VTA replies with a `permissionDenied` **envelope**, which an approver wallet has no reason to recognise, and logs nothing — the `trust-task received` line and every `consent.decision` audit row live *past* the gate. So this:

```
consent-diag: no grant found for (requester, digest) …
consent-diag: REUSING the outstanding pending … waiting on the approver's grant
audit: action="consent.required" … outcome="pending:reasked"
   ×N forever
```

was indistinguishable from a decision that was never delivered — while the human had approved, the wallet had sent, and the VTA had discarded it.

## The fix

- **`trust_tasks::ceremony`** (new) — the ceremony predicate, lifted out of `policy_gate` where it was private. That privacy *was* the bug: only one of the two gates in front of a handler knew what a ceremony task is. Both now share it.
- **`messaging::auth::auth_for_trust_task_envelope`** — the single entry point both transports use for the trust-task surface. `auth_from_did` plus one carve-out: when the ACL turns a sender away **and** the envelope names a ceremony task, dispatch proceeds on the proven sender DID over `Role::Monitor` with no contexts. Authorized nowhere, no session row minted.
- **Both transports name the sender and type URI when they refuse**, so a task the VTA rejected can be told apart from one that never arrived. `handle_decision` already argues the case for exactly this line one layer down.

A fallback, not an override:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| named approver, no ACL entry, decision | dispatched, zero authority |
| DID in no approver set, decision | refused (see hardening below) |
| named approver, `dids/update` | refused, as before |
| unparseable body | refused — can't talk past the ACL by being malformed |
| enrolled admin, decision | keeps its real claims, no downgrade |
| **expired** ACL grant, decision | through, but the lapsed admin role is not resurrected |
| store/session error (not `Forbidden`) | propagates — infrastructure faults are not downgraded |

## Second commit: the carve-out has a floor

The carve-out costs one durable write. A decision that verifies but cites a digest with no live pending records `consent.decision / denied:no_pending`, and audit retention is time-based (`retention_days`), not size-capped — so without a filter, anyone who can reach the mediator could flood the audit log with rows that outlive the incident by weeks. Not privilege escalation; the claim still reaches nothing. But it is a capability that did not exist when the ACL refused those senders outright.

For a consent decision the eligible population is an in-memory config read: membership of some configured approver set. That is exactly the population the carve-out serves, so the filter costs nothing in function while shrinking the reachable set from "any DID" to "the DIDs the operator named". The handler still enforces the specific set the pending named — a floor, not the decision.

Step-up `approve-response` stays unfiltered, deliberately, on two findings:
- Its authorized signer is `pending.approver`, recorded at mint and **not** required to hold an ACL entry — the delegated phone-as-authorizer. A blanket "approvers must be enrolled" rule would break it.
- It needs no floor: `handle_approve_response` writes no audit row on `challenge_unknown`, `subject_mismatch` or `approver_unauthorized`, so an unknown sender leaves nothing durable behind.

Also: a refused ceremony task now says which of the two enrolments is missing. An approver added to the approver set but not the ACL, and one added to neither, are the same silence from the wallet's side.

## Scope

REST is untouched — `/api/trust-tasks` still requires a JWT. The approver paths (browser plugin, mobile) are DIDComm/TSP; widening REST would mean route-level auth changes and is not needed here.

## Tests

790 lib tests pass; clippy clean; `rest` / `didcomm` / `rest,didcomm` / `rest,didcomm,tsp,webvh` all build warning-free.

New coverage:
- `messaging/auth.rs` — 8 gate cases, one per row of the table above plus the approver-set floor, the step-up exemption, and "no session row is minted".
- `trust_tasks/ceremony.rs` — the predicate, the pre-auth `type` peek, and `ceremony_claims` asserted to reach nothing.
- `trust_tasks/task_consent.rs` — end-to-end: signs a real decision as an unenrolled `did:key`, runs it through the **actual** transport gate, and asserts a consumable grant lands for the requester. That is the line that was never reached in the field.

## Verification

Found against a live VTA where the browser-plugin approver was in `webvh-approvers` but not the ACL:

```
$ pnm acl get did:key:z6Mkngm…Ufke
✗ not found: ACL entry not found for DID: did:key:z6Mkngm…Ufke
```

That deployment is deliberately left unfixed so this can be confirmed end-to-end against a real wallet once merged.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- `pnm-browser-plugin`: `onInboundMessage` drops the VTA's rejection envelope with no log (`offscreen.ts:1878`). This PR stops the rejection happening; the wallet should still surface one when it does.

adopting it would oblige the community to echo the credential back to the party
that just sent it. `vtc/join-requests/accept` has the same delivery shape. Both
are correct as they stand.

**The real near-duplicate is `vta/credentials/issue`**, whose response is
`IssuedCredential`'s members and required set plus `supersedes` and `ext`. It
cannot `$ref` the shared definition: that definition sets
`additionalProperties: false`, and under `allOf` each subschema is evaluated
against the whole object, so the ref would reject the two extra members.

## Why nothing is restructured

Removing the unused `$def` is a breaking change to a shared component (§6.6 item
1) requiring a new component version, and §6.6 item 3 then requires each of the
three consuming specifications to publish a new version to re-pin. That is one
component version and three spec versions to delete something nobody uses.

So this is documentation. `IssuedCredential` now states that it is an *issuance*
receipt, that a delivery task returns something different and must not echo the
credential back, and why `vta/credentials/issue` states its members inline. That
spec's response says the same from its side, so whichever one a reader lands on
tells them the relationship.

Editorial only — descriptions, in place, permitted for a draft artifact by §5.2.
No member, constraint or required set changes; the generated bindings pick up the
new doc comments and nothing else.

title: feat(didcomm-v1): reference implementation for the DIDComm v1 binding
body:
Credo — and therefore essentially every Aries-lineage wallet — speaks DIDComm v1
and only v1. Our DIDComm binding targets v2.1, so those stacks had no way to
carry a Trust Task at all. This is the crate side of closing that, built on
`affinidi-messaging-didcomm-v1` (TDK #687).

Thin and shaped like `trust-tasks-didcomm`, so an implementation can drive both
protocols through the same seam.

## ⚠️ Carriage: a decision that needs @bmiller59's view

v2.1 has an obvious slot for the document — the message `body`. **v1 has none.**
The payload is flattened at top level beside `@id`, `@type` and the decorators,
and RFC 0095 types `basic-message`'s `content` as a *string* for human display,
which Credo renders as chat text. The TDK supports three carriages and endorses
none:

> Whichever the binding picks, it must say so normatively: unlike v2.1, where the
> message `body` is the obvious home, a v1 basic-message has no self-evident slot
> and two implementations will otherwise choose differently.

| option | why not |
|---|---|
| JSON-in-`content` | Reaches every v1 agent, but each Trust Task renders in a wallet as a wall of double-encoded JSON. That's the *primary* Aries experience, not an edge case. |
| Sibling top-level member | Keeps `content` readable and nothing rejects it, but invents a slot no Aries reader looks in. |
| **`~attach`** ✅ | Idiomatic Aries home for a structured payload; document stays JSON rather than a string inside a string; `content` stays free for a summary. |

```json
{
  "@type": "did:sov:BzCbsNYhMrjHiqZDTUASHg;spec/basicmessage/1.0/message",
  "~thread": { "thid": "…" },
  "content": "Trust Task: https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1",
  "~attach": [{ "@id": "trust-task", "mime-type": "application/json",
                "data": { "json": { "id": "…", "type": "…", "payload": {} } } }]
}
```

**Not ratified.** `bindings/didcomm-v1/0.1` is Brendan's to author; this is a
proposal his spec can adopt or overturn. Nothing depends on the crate yet, so the
choice is cheap to change — that's why we built rather than waited.

## What v1 forces that v2.1 did not

**Attribution takes an extra step.** A v2.1 envelope authenticates a DID. A v1
envelope carries **no DID at all** — a bare base58 verkey, with the verkey→DID
binding held as connection state. So there's a third failure mode with no v2.1
counterpart: `UnknownSenderBinding`, an envelope that's cryptographically sound
but attributable to nobody this agent knows.

Kept distinct from `UnauthenticatedSender` deliberately. One means nobody signed
it; the other means somebody did and we can't name them. The operator response
differs — a missing connection record versus a hostile message — and collapsing
them hides the first behind the second. Both map to `proofRequired`, since
neither yields a party to attribute the document to.

## Thread mapping

Per §9.1 and matching `bindings/didcomm/0.2`: `threadId` ↔ `thid`,
`parentThreadId` ↔ `pthid`, populated from the framework members, compared only
where both are explicitly present.

Two details the TDK made easy to get right:

- **`explicit_thid()` not `effective_thid()`.** A defaulted `thid` is a value the
  transport synthesised from `@id`, not one the sender asserted. Comparing
  against it would manufacture disagreements out of conforming messages.
- **`is_basic_message()` not `typ ==`.** v1 message types have two
  interchangeable document URIs and Credo emits the `https://didcomm.org` one by
  default, so exact comparison silently drops conforming peers.

## Verification

9 crate tests — attachment round trip, thread mapping both directions,
human-readable `content` (asserting it is *not* JSON), and both
unattributable-sender cases. Workspace: 31 suites, clippy clean,
`cargo package` succeeds.

Added to `publish.yml`'s watch paths and publish order, after `trust-tasks-rs`.

- `bindings/didcomm-v1/0.1` — Brendan's to author.
- Interop against a live Credo agent. The TDK has fixtures and a harness under

title: ci: say what a release did, and catch first-publish crates before they 403
body:
Two releases in a row failed at `cargo publish`, and both needed the raw log to
diagnose. Neither stranded anything — but that was luck.

## The recurring failure

A crate that doesn't yet exist on crates.io **cannot** be published from CI:

```
403 Forbidden: Trusted Publishing tokens do not support creating new crates.
Publish the crate manually, first.
```

There's no crate for a Trusted Publisher to attach to. The decide step treated a
404 as "never published, so publish it" and handed it to `cargo publish`, which
403'd mid-run. `trust-tasks-capability-client` hit it, then
`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`.

Now they're separated up front and reported with the exact commands — and
**everything else still publishes**. Failing the whole release because one new
crate needs a manual bootstrap would turn a one-time chore into a blocked
release. The job fails at the end so the run is red and the chore isn't missed.

## The silent part

`set -euo pipefail` around a bare loop meant a failure killed the step with no
statement of what had already gone out. Both times the answer happened to be
"nothing you'd miss" — once the failure was last, once the remainder were
no-ops. A first-time crate in the *middle* of a real multi-crate release would
have left a genuinely partial state with the log offering only an exit code.

The loop now records outcomes and writes a job summary:

```
**Published:** trust-tasks-rs trust-tasks-https
**Failed:** trust-tasks-didcomm
**Not attempted:** trust-tasks-proof trust-tasks-tsp
```

It still stops at the first failure, deliberately — the crates are ordered by
dependency, so continuing risks publishing a dependent against a version of
`trust-tasks-rs` that never landed. The change is that the partial state is
*stated* rather than inferred.

## Verification

Shell logic exercised under bash against a simulated mid-list failure:

```
published a
published b
**Published:**  a b
**Failed:** c
**Not attempted:** d e
(exits 1)
```

(My first run of that simulation was under zsh, which doesn't word-split
unquoted variables, so the loop saw one item and the test was meaningless. The
workflow runs bash; re-tested there.)

Workflow YAML parses and all eight steps resolve in order.

title: feat(bindings): map DIDComm thread headers, and release framework 0.3 as 0.3.0
body:
Last of the framework 0.3 changes, plus the coordinated release the previous
three deferred.

## `bindings/didcomm/0.2`

`0.1` stated that the framework consumed no DIDComm headers, which left `thid`
and the framework's `threadId` free to disagree with nothing noticing. SPEC §9.1
(added in #183) requires a binding that maps them to state the mapping — this is
that mapping.

| Framework member | DIDComm header |
|---|---|
| `threadId` | `thid` |
| `parentThreadId` | `pthid` |

Producers **SHOULD** populate the headers *from* the members. Consumers compare
only where **both** are explicitly present, and reject a disagreement with
`malformedRequest` — **not** `identityMismatch`, which is reserved for a
contested party identity and drags in §8.1's response-suppression rules. A
thread disagreement contests nobody's identity.

The both-present scoping is the substance of the rule, not a hedge: DIDComm's
`thid` defaults to the DIDComm message `id`, the framework's `threadId` falls
back to the *Trust Task document*'s `id`, and §2 of the binding is explicit that
those are independent. An unconditional equality rule would reject exchanges
that conform perfectly on both layers.

MINOR increment, so the envelope type is preserved per the binding's own §6 — a
`0.1` consumer still recognises a `0.2` producer's messages.

### A real bug this surfaced

`pack_trust_task` set `thid` from `doc.id`. That's correct only for a document
that *opens* an exchange, and wrong for every response, which carries the
originating `threadId` — so every document started a fresh DIDComm thread
instead of continuing one. Now takes `threadId` falling back to `id`, which is
§4.9's own rule.

## Release 0.3.0

Framework 0.3 is complete:

| | |
|---|---|
| #179 | §4.9.1 — naming an exchange from outside the framework |
| #183 | `parentThreadId` + the §9.1 transport-mapping requirement |
| #184 | Per-variant proof declarations |
| #185 | Self-describing error responses |
| this | The DIDComm thread mapping |

One workspace event, exactly as the #178 versioning policy warns:

```
trust-tasks-rs                 0.2.60 → 0.3.0
trust-tasks-https               0.2.2 → 0.3.0
trust-tasks-didcomm             0.2.0 → 0.3.0
trust-tasks-proof               0.2.2 → 0.3.0
trust-tasks-tsp                 0.2.2 → 0.3.0
trust-tasks-capability-client   0.1.0 → 0.2.0   (its own line)
@openvtc/trust-tasks           0.2.60 → 0.3.0
```

The leading component moves because `TrustTask` gained `parent_thread_id` and
`ErrorPayload` gained `in_response_to` — both break struct-literal
construction. The five dependents' requirements move to `version = "0.3"`.

### ⚠️ Behavioural changes

Full migration notes in the changelog; the two that will be noticed:

- **Error responses are emitted as `trust-task-error/0.3`**, not `0.2`. The
  runtimes populate `inResponseTo` and `0.2`'s schema is
  `additionalProperties: false`. §5.2 forward-minor means a `0.2` consumer
  SHOULD accept it.
- **`trust-tasks-didcomm` continues a thread** rather than starting one per
  document.

## Verification

- Registry clean — 286 specs, 402 example documents
- `cargo test --workspace` 29 suites; 3 new binding tests
- clippy clean; `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs` succeeds
- TS 43/43, smoke passes, infra 14/14
- Codegen idempotent both sides
- Workspace resolves with all five dependents on `version = "0.3"`

## On merge

`publish.yml` releases all seven: `trust-tasks-rs` first, then the four bindings
in dependency order, then npm. This is the first release since the policy was
written down, so worth watching that the ordering holds.

title: test(vtc): make the join_didcomm credential-delivery failure diagnosable
body:
`didcomm_join_round_trips_submit_manifest_status_approve_and_vmc_delivery` has
failed on CI at least **three times across unrelated PRs** (#903, #904 — one of
them a diff that was purely DIDComm framing in a different crate). Every failure
produced the same line, and no way to act on it:

```
panicked at vtc-service/tests/join_didcomm.rs:288:14:
admission credential delivered over DIDComm
```

**No production behaviour changes here, and this does not attempt a fix.** It
removes the three reasons the failure has never been attributable.

## What I ruled out

| Hypothesis | Verdict |
|---|---|
| R1.1 silent drop | **No** — `send_to_member` uses `Delivery::Guaranteed`: durable outbox, retries. Not a bare send |
| Idempotency-key collision deduping push #2 | **No** — `deliver_credentials` mints a fresh UUID per credential; `push_to_holder` uses it as the message id |
| Arrival-order race | **No** — already handled; the test collects both and searches |
| Runner slowness *(the test's own explanation)* | **Doesn't fit** — see below |

The slowness story is the one worth retiring. The bound is already **60s** on a
test that completes in ~23s on CI, and the client polls every **300ms** — so a
failure is ~200 consecutive empty polls. That is a message that isn't there, not
one that's late.

Six local runs did not reproduce it. **No root cause is claimed.**

## Three blind spots, removed

**1. No tracing subscriber.** These tests installed none, so the service's
`warn!("membership-credential delivery failed on approve…")` went nowhere. That
warn is the *only* report of a failed push — the caller deliberately swallows the
error, because the credentials are already issued and returned inline, so a
delivery failure must not unwind the decision. Result: a silent send failure and
a lost frame were indistinguishable.

`init_tracing()` installs one, filtering `lsm_tree` — its temp-dir teardown emits
a screenful of harmless cleanup warnings *precisely when a test fails*, which
would bury the line that matters. `RUST_LOG` overrides.

**2. The assertion couldn't tell "got 0" from "got 1".** `deliver_credentials` is
a sequential loop with `?`: a failure on the first push sends **zero**, a failure
on the second sends **one**. Two different bugs, identical symptom. The panic now
names the index, the timeout, how many arrived, and which explanation applies.

**3. `recv_matching` discarded every pickup error.** `if let Ok(Some(..)) = next`
swallowed up to ~200 `Err`s per failure, so a broken socket and an unsent message
looked the same. Now counted and reported on timeout — still non-fatal, since a
transient pickup error is expected and retrying is the point.

## Verified against a real failure, not assumed

Timeout shortened to 3s and the loop extended by one, to force the path:

```
admission credential 3/2 not delivered over DIDComm within 3s (2 already received).
The first arrived and the second did not, so the VTC either failed on the second
`push_to_holder` (again warn-only) or the frame was lost between the mediator and
this client.
```

`lsm_tree` lines in that output: **0**. Restored to 60s / two credentials; the
suite passes.

## What this buys

The next CI failure produces one data point that settles it: whether the VTC sent
zero, sent one, or sent two that didn't arrive — and, if the service logged a
send failure, the reason. That is what a fix needs and what nobody has had.

Deliberately **not** done: raising the timeout. If the message never arrives, a
bigger bound just fails slower.

## Pre-merge checklist (guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — n/a, test-only
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — the poll loop's bound is unchanged
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — unchanged behaviour; errors are now *counted* rather than discarded, still non-fatal
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — unchanged
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — none
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — **the point of the PR**: a swallowed delivery failure and a swallowed pickup error are both now surfaced
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none

Takes `0.11.52`; #905 already claims `0.11.51`.

title: feat(framework): let an error response say what it reports on (§8.2)
body:
Third of the framework 0.3 changes, and proposal item 2 from #173 — the one
cred-spec's evidence model actually turns on.

## The gap

An error response correlated back to its originating document by `threadId`
alone. That works between the two parties to an exchange and identifies nothing
to anyone else: `threadId` is opaque, and the payload named neither the
specification the failure occurred under nor the instance that triggered it.

A party handed a retained error saw this, and could not tell what failed:

```json
{ "code": "taskFailed", "retryable": false }
```

For an *extended* code the slug namespace (§8.5) at least hinted at the family.
For any of the standard codes of §8.3 there was no signal of origin at all.

@bmiller59 hit this directly: cred-spec's outcome document travels with a
credential presentation to a verifier who was never party to the exchange, so
an error reaching that verifier was unusable as evidence.

## The member

`inResponseTo` carries the reported-on document's `typeUri` — **including any
`#request` / `#response` fragment**, which is what tells a consumer whose
semantics apply to an extended code — and its `id`, which §4.3 makes globally
unique and never reused, so it names one *instance* where `threadId` names an
*exchange*.

```json
{
  "code": "proofRequired",
  "inResponseTo": {
    "typeUri": "https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1",
    "id": "urn:uuid:4f3c9e2a-1b81-4d3e-9b51-7a3c89e3d1f2"
  },
  "retryable": false
}
```

**SHOULD** in general; **MUST** where the error will be retained, replayed, or
relied upon beyond the original producer — the same condition under which §4.7.1
makes a `proof` mandatory, and for the same reason. An error that can be
attributed but not identified is not evidence of anything.

## Additive now, required later

Published as `trust-task-error/0.3` with both members **optional**, so a 0.2
consumer's output stays valid 0.3. That's a migration allowance, not a design
position — a future major version is expected to require them, with 0.1/0.2
retired once consumers have moved. Adding an optional member is
backwards-compatible, so §5.2 makes this a MINOR increment rather than a break.

## ⚠️ The libraries now emit 0.3

Both runtimes populate the member, so both moved from emitting
`trust-task-error/0.2` to `0.3` — 0.2's payload schema is
`additionalProperties: false`, and a document carrying `inResponseTo` would not
validate against it. §5.2's forward-minor rule means a 0.2 consumer **SHOULD**
accept a 0.3 document, which is the sanctioned path, but it is a behavioural
change and part of why this belongs in the 0.3.0 library release.

Population happens in the **document builders**, not the callers. The builder is
the only place that reliably holds the originating document, and a member that's
only sometimes present is worth far less than one that's always there. A
caller-supplied value is preserved.

## Disclosure

Under `identityMismatch` the `id` is **withheld**. Per §8.1 the response is
addressed to the transport-authenticated sender rather than the in-band
`issuer`, and that party did not necessarily compose the document whose
identifier would be echoed. The `typeUri` stays — it isn't identifying. Both
runtimes enforce this and both have a test for it.

The 0.3 spec also documents when to omit the member entirely: where the
attempted task is itself sensitive, a partly-populated value is worse than none.

## Verification

- Registry clean — 286 specs, 402 example documents
- `cargo test --workspace` 29 suites; **3 new** integration tests (names the
  document, withholds the id under `identityMismatch`, preserves a
  caller-supplied value)
- TS 43/43 — **5 new**, mirroring the Rust set plus one asserting the emitted
  Type URI is 0.3
- clippy clean. The dispatcher's captured request metadata became a
  `RequestOrigin` struct: it had grown past clippy's argument limit, and
  bundling it beat silencing the lint
- Codegen idempotent both sides; smoke test passes

**No version bump** — the last 0.3 change is `bindings/didcomm/0.2`, and the
0.3.0 seven-crate release follows it.

title: fix(messaging): an unknown inbound protocol is dropped, not fatal
body:
`affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.6 added a `Protocol::DIDCommV1` variant and marked
the enum `#[non_exhaustive]`. Both inbound routers stopped compiling:

```
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `_` not covered
  --> vta-service/src/messaging/service.rs:310:11
  --> vtc-service/src/messaging.rs:341:23
```

## Not the fix rustc suggests

rustc proposes `_ => todo!()`. That would be a **remotely triggerable panic** —
this match runs on every inbound frame off the mediator socket, so any peer
sending a protocol we don't implement yet takes the listener down. Both routers
warn and drop.

## DIDComm v1 is not a flavour of v2.1

`DIDCommV1` (Aries RFC 0019) gets its own arm rather than folding into the
`DIDComm` one. Upstream is explicit that the two *"share no wire format, no
algorithms, and no identifier scheme"*, and both services speak v2.1 only.

In `vtc-service` this is load-bearing, not cosmetic. Its `Protocol::DIDComm` arm
is `{}` and falls **through** to the v2.1 parse below, so an unhandled variant
reaching it would be parsed as a v2.1 plaintext and dropped *silently* — which is
exactly the failure the comment directly above that match already records for
TSP:

> the DIDComm branch below would fail to parse the payload and drop the frame
> silently, which is what happened before this

The new arms `continue`.

## Why this class keeps landing

Second `#[non_exhaustive]` break in two days — #902 carried the `UnpackMetadata`
one. Both were invisible until a dependency moved. The attribute exists so
*additive* upstream changes aren't breaking; a `match` without a wildcard opts
back into breakage. Worth preferring a wildcard on any upstream enum matched in a
hot inbound path, `#[non_exhaustive]` or not.

## Verification

`affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.5 → 0.1.6.

| target | feature sets |
|---|---|
| workspace | `--all-features`, `--all-targets` (test targets included) |
| `vta-service` | `--no-default-features`, and each of `didcomm`, `rest`, `tsp`, `didcomm,tsp`, `rest,didcomm,webvh,tsp` |

`cargo fmt --check`, `check-version-bumps.sh`, `check-changelogs.sh` clean.

## Pre-merge checklist (guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — **directly on point**: this is what the change is for. An unknown protocol no longer aborts (or, under rustc's suggestion, panics) the inbound loop; it logs and continues
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — unchanged
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire types changed
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — an unrecognised protocol is dropped, not optimistically parsed
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — each drop warns with the protocol named, rather than vanishing
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — no mutations

title: feat(framework): let a specification declare proof per document variant
body:
Second of the framework 0.3 changes. Proposal item 3 from #173.

## The gap

§7.3 item 8 was one declaration covering every variant, so a spec needing a
proof on one had to require it on both. The two are relied upon differently:

- a **response** retained as evidence by a party outside the original exchange
  can need a proof where the request that triggered it does not
- a **request** that destroys state needs to be attributable while the
  acknowledgement it returns protects nothing

#174 hit this directly. Twelve specs moved to `proof: REQUIRED`, and several had
authors who'd reasoned — correctly — that an envelope proof adds nothing over an
inner one. With no way to say "required on the response, not the request", the
stricter value went on both.

`proofRequirement` now accepts either the existing single `requirement` or a
per-variant `request` / `response` pair. Omitting `response` takes the
`request`'s value, so an omission can never weaken a variant.

## The floor splits with it

`checkProofFloor` applied one floor to everything. Each class now constrains the
variant it actually describes:

```
sideEffects.level: destructive  ┐  the REQUEST causes the effect
exposure.actsAsSubject: true    ┘  → the request must be proven

exposure.discloses: secret         the RESPONSE carries the material
                                   → the response must be proven
```

Measured across the registry — 55 spec versions are touched by a floor:

| | |
|---|---|
| **40** | could relax their **response** |
| **9** | could relax their **request** |
| **6** | declare both classes — neither relaxes |

## A correction I owe

That last row matters, because it contradicts how I argued for this change.

I said repeatedly — including in a comment on #173 — that per-variant is what
`credential-exchange/present` needs, and that it wants
`{request: RECOMMENDED, response: REQUIRED}`. It doesn't. `present` declares
`actsAsSubject: true` **and** `discloses: secret`, so both floors apply and
neither variant relaxes. Same for `vtc/auth/admin-session`, the other example I
used. **The two specs I built the argument on are precisely the two this doesn't
help.**

The mechanism is still clearly worth having — 49 of 55 gain something — but the
motivating example was wrong, and I'd rather say so here than let it stand. I'll
post a correction on #173.

## No spec changes

Every existing declaration keeps its meaning, both generators produce
**byte-identical** output, and relaxing any variant is a per-spec decision for
its owners — not something to sweep in with the mechanism.

## The error variant stays undeclarable

An error response's `type` resolves to `trust-task-error`, a *different*
specification, and §7.2 item 7 resolves the requirement from the specification
the `type` names. A declaration in a task spec can't reach it, so offering an
`error` key would promise something unenforceable. Item 8 now says so explicitly
instead of leaving it ambiguous — making error responses attributable needs them
to name their originating specification first, which is the next 0.3 change.

## Verification

Proved end-to-end by temporarily declaring `{request: REQUIRED, response:
RECOMMENDED}` on `keys/sign`:

```
req: const IS_PROOF_REQUIRED: bool = true;     res: (constant absent → false)
req: isProofRequired: true,                    res: isProofRequired: false,
```

Floor tested both directions — relaxing the request on an `actsAsSubject` spec
fails the build with a variant-specific message; relaxing its response passes.

Registry clean (285 specs, 397 example documents) · `cargo test --workspace` 29
suites · clippy clean · TS 38/38 · smoke passes · infra 14/14 · **no codegen
drift**.

**No version bump** — still accumulating for the single 0.3.0 seven-crate
release, per #183.

title: fix(webvh): VTA→DID-hosting DIDComm uses the Trust-Task envelope binding
body:
The last and largest of the envelope-binding fixes (#901, #903).
`webvh_didcomm.rs` sent **seven** DID-management verbs with the *task* type as
the DIDComm message type, where `trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE` is required
with the `TrustTask` in the body.

`did/check-name`, `did/register` (which also carries publish), `did/delete`,
`agent-name/{update,remove,list,check}`.

## Why this one was invisible

Unlike the device pushes, **this never broke anything.** did-hosting's control
plane accepts both framings — `build_control_router` routes the bare `MSG_*`
types *and* `ENVELOPE_TYPE`, and the envelope path reaches the same
`dispatch_did_op` table via `bridge_did_management` — so publish, register,
delete and the agent-name verbs all worked, and still do.

The defect was **latent**. The moment the host retires bare-type acceptance —
its stated direction — every one of these verbs starts timing out at 30s with no
diagnostic. That is not hypothetical: it is exactly what the retired
`did/publish/0.1` did in affinidi-webvh-service#144, one verb at a time.

## The shape

`send_task` is now the only place this module names a DIDComm message type, and
it names the envelope both ways. Each verb passes just its task URI, so **no call
site can put a task type on the wire**.

**Outbound** — `build_outbound` returns the `(message_type, document)` pair:
envelope on the message, task type on the document, payload untouched.

**Inbound** — reply handling had to move. On this binding every reply arrives as
`ENVELOPE_TYPE`, so `send_and_wait`'s outer type check can no longer tell success
from rejection. `unwrap_envelope_reply` discriminates on the *document's* type:

| document type | result |
|---|---|
| `<task>#response` | its `payload` |
| `did/problem-report/0.1` | typed `AppError`, via the **same** `problem_report_to_app_error` table the bare framing uses (now `pub(crate)`) |
| `trust-task-error/0.x` | 502 — the framework refused the *envelope*, not the task |
| anything else | 502 naming both types |

Routing the problem report through the shared table is what keeps
`path-unavailable` a **409** instead of collapsing to 502 — the exact regression
that table was introduced to fix. A host rejection must not change status
depending on which framing carried it.

`trust-task-error` is matched by **prefix**: did-hosting emits `0.1` for a
body-parse failure and `0.2` from the typed §7.2 pipeline, in the same
conversation.

## Prerequisite — already shipped

**affinidi-webvh-service#155** gave the host's envelope path the anti-replay gate
its bare-type path already had (`check_and_insert` had two production callers,
neither on the envelope path). Both framings reach the same state-changing
operations, so without it this PR would have worked *and* silently dropped replay
protection for `delete`, `change-owner` and `register`.

Merged and on `upstream/main` as `f7a70a6` before this was written.

⚠️ **Deploy #155 before merging this.** Merged is not deployed; the ordering
constraint is on the running host, not the branch.

## Tests

Six new. The outbound one asserts **both** halves off `build_outbound`, which is
what keeps it from being circular: `send_task` destructures that return, so
restoring the defect means bypassing the function rather than editing one
argument.

Verified against the *defect*, not just the fix:

```
assertion `left == right` failed: the DIDComm message must carry the binding's envelope type
  left: "https://trusttasks.org/spec/did-management/did/check-name/0.1"
 right: "https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope"
```

Worth stating plainly: an earlier draft of these tests covered only the document
builder and did **not** catch that regression — I checked, found the gap, and
restructured until they did. Given that this whole workstream exists because a
test pinned the defect rather than caught it, "the tests pass" was not a
sufficient claim to stop on.

`cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets` clean. Compiles at
`--no-default-features` and with each of `didcomm`, `rest`, `tsp`, `didcomm,tsp`,
`rest,didcomm,webvh,tsp`.

## Not in scope

**TSP is untouched, deliberately.** It carries the document bytes directly
(`serde_json::to_vec(doc)` → `send_routed`), so the envelope is a property of the
DIDComm binding, not of the task. Applying it there would break a working
transport to fix a latent one.

`webvh_didcomm` and `trust-tasks-didcomm` are both ungated, so the
`ENVELOPE_TYPE` import needs no `#[cfg]` — verified across the feature matrix
above rather than assumed.

**Adopting `pack_trust_task` is designed, not done.** It generates the envelope
id internally (`Message::new`) and returns only the JWE, while the bridge's reply
correlation *is* that id — peers reply `.thid(message.id)`. Adopting it as-is
makes every `send_and_wait` time out. Written up in
`design-docs/vti-pack-trust-task-adoption.md`, which recommends a typed seam on
`DIDCommBridge` instead and names the upstream ask (return the id, or accept a
caller-supplied one).

## Merge order

1. affinidi-webvh-service#155 — merged ✅, **needs deploying**
2. #903 (device pushes) — independent of this
3. **this PR**

## Pre-merge checklist (guide §9)

body:
fix(webvh): VTA→DID-hosting DIDComm uses the Trust-Task envelope binding (#904)

* fix(webvh): VTA->DID-hosting DIDComm uses the Trust-Task envelope binding

webvh_didcomm.rs sent seven DID-management verbs with the task type as the
DIDComm message type, where trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE is required with
the TrustTask in the body.

Unlike the device pushes in #901 and #903, this never broke anything. The host's
control plane accepts both framings -- build_control_router routes the bare MSG_*
types and ENVELOPE_TYPE, and the envelope path reaches the same dispatch_did_op
table via bridge_did_management -- so publish, register, delete and the
agent-name verbs all worked. The defect was latent. The moment the host retires
bare-type acceptance, every one of these verbs starts timing out at 30s with no
diagnostic, exactly as the retired did/publish/0.1 did
(affinidi-webvh-service#144).

send_task is now the only place this module names a DIDComm message type, and it
names the envelope both ways; each verb passes just its task URI, so no call site
can put a task type on the wire. build_outbound returns the (message_type,
document) pair -- envelope on the message, task in the document, payload
untouched.

Reply handling had to move. On this binding every reply arrives as
ENVELOPE_TYPE, so send_and_wait's outer type check can no longer tell success
from rejection; unwrap_envelope_reply discriminates on the document's own type
instead. A did/problem-report goes through the same problem_report_to_app_error
table the bare framing uses (now pub(crate)), so a host rejection keeps its
status -- path-unavailable stays a 409 rather than collapsing to 502. A
trust-task-error is a 502: the framework refused the envelope, not the task, so
it is not an outcome a caller can act on. It is matched by prefix because the
version floats between 0.1 and 0.2 within one conversation.

affinidi-webvh-service#155 shipped first and is why this is safe: it gave the
host's envelope path the anti-replay gate its bare-type path already had. Both
framings reach the same state-changing operations, so without it this change
would have worked and silently dropped replay protection for delete,
change-owner and register.

Six tests. The outbound one asserts both halves off build_outbound, which is what
keeps it from being circular -- send_task destructures that return, so restoring
the defect means bypassing the function rather than editing an argument. Checked
against the defect: an earlier draft tested only the document builder and did not
catch the regression, so the tests were restructured until they did.

TSP untouched -- it carries document bytes directly, so the envelope is a
property of the DIDComm binding.

title: feat(framework): add the optional parentThreadId envelope member (§4.9.2)
body:
First of the framework 0.3 changes. Answers the nesting question @bmiller59
raised in #173.

## The gap

A `threadId` names one exchange and expresses no relationship to any other, but
exchanges nest — a Trust Task run to complete a step of a broader interaction is
still its own exchange with its own thread. Nothing recorded that, so a party
holding a document from the inner exchange couldn't find the exchange it was
conducted within.

Specifications were solving it privately. cred-spec linked the two halves of a
witnessed exchange with a payload member because there was no `pthid`
equivalent, and this registry already carries 23 specs with hand-rolled
correlation members. That produces per-family conventions for something the
framework should say once — the same drift §8.5 accumulated before family
namespaces.

## What it is

Optional, taking `threadId`'s posture: no normative validation semantics,
consumers **MUST NOT** reject on it alone, and a producer **SHOULD** carry it
onto every document of the inner exchange — response and error response included
— because the whole exchange shares one parent. A producer **MUST NOT** set it
equal to the document's own `threadId`.

**One level of containment, deliberately**, matching DIDComm's single `pthid`.
Deeper ancestry needs the intervening documents, and a half-defined chain is
worse than an explicit payload structure for specs that genuinely need one.

## What it is *not*

It is **not** the anchoring rule. §4.9.1 already says a citation naming an
exchange as evidence must name the *innermost* exchange that attests the event.
That stands on its own and doesn't depend on this member — which is exactly why
it shipped separately in #179 and unblocked cred-spec without waiting for this.
§4.9.1 is touched only where it previously claimed the framework cannot
represent containment.

This member is a **navigation aid**: it lets a holder of an inner document walk
outward. It never changes which exchange attests an event.

## Transport alignment

New §9.1 bullet — a binding mapping the framework's thread members onto its own
correlation identifiers MUST state the mapping, and MUST require agreement only
when **both** values are explicitly present.

That scoping is load-bearing. The two layers identify different things and
default into their own identifier spaces: DIDComm's `thid` falls back to the
DIDComm message id, which `bindings/didcomm/0.1` is explicit is *not* the Trust
Task document's `id`. Unconditional equality would fail conforming exchanges. A
disagreement is `malformedRequest`, not `identityMismatch` — no party's identity
is in dispute.

`bindings/didcomm/0.1` declines to map at all and remains conforming; the
mapping arrives with a new binding version, as its own PR.

## Scope

| | |
|---|---|
| SPEC.md | §2, §4.2, §4.9.1 correction, new §4.9.2 + worked example, §4.10, §6.3, §7.1, §9.1, Appendix B |
| Schema | `_framework/0.3/trust-task.schema.json`. 0.1/0.2 already accept it — §4.2 permits additional top-level members — so this is recognition, not permission |
| Rust | `TrustTask::parent_thread_id`, carried by `respond_with`, `reject_with_recipient`, and the dispatcher's routing-time error builder |
| TypeScript | `TrustTaskDocument.parentThreadId`, carried by `respondWith`/`rejectWithRecipient`, assigned conditionally so an absent parent stays **absent** rather than an explicit `undefined` |

## Verification

- Registry clean; corpus check extended to 0.3 and now validates **397** example
  documents — it picked up the new §4.9.2 example automatically
- `cargo test --workspace` 29 suites, clippy clean; 3 new Rust tests (carried
  onto both response kinds, omitted from the wire when unset, round-trips under
  its wire name)
- TS 38/38 (5 new), smoke test passes, `tsc` clean
- No codegen drift either side

## No version bump — deliberate

Adding a public field to `TrustTask` breaks struct-literal construction, so under
#178 this is a leading-component bump. That's a **seven-crate release**, and
per-variant proof and self-describing error responses are both due in 0.3 too.
The bump lands with the last of them so the cost is paid once. Publishing is
version-gated, so nothing ships from `main` meanwhile.

Refs #173

title: docs(infra): the real-404 fix depends on the bucket policy, not just CloudFront
body:
#181 was necessary but not sufficient. Applying it to the live distribution left
the original bug intact — an unknown Type URI still returned the shell under a
200.

## Why

The remaining `403 -> /index.html as 200` mapping, plus the bucket policy. With
CloudFront + OAC granting only `s3:GetObject`, S3 **cannot distinguish a missing
key from a forbidden one** and answers `403 AccessDenied` instead of 404. The
403 mapping converts that straight back into the site shell under a success
status.

## Fixed on the distribution

Granted the CloudFront principal `s3:ListBucket`, scoped to the same `SourceArn`
condition as the existing `s3:GetObject` statement — purely additive:

```json
{
  "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontListBucketForRealNotFound",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" },
  "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::trusttasks-794038245035-us-east-1-an",
  "Condition": { "ArnLike": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::…:distribution/E2JUK67AKK23KC" } }
}
```

It's narrower than it sounds: CloudFront never issues a list operation on a
viewer's behalf and the distribution offers no way to trigger one. The grant
only changes which error S3 returns for a missing key.

**All eight `verify.sh` checks now pass against the live site**, and every SPA
route was re-checked (`/`, `/categories`, `/about`, `/registry`,
`/specification`, `/bindings`, `/ecosystem`) — all 200.

```
ok  /spec/trust-task/0.2                 application/schema+json
ok  /spec/acl/grant/0.1                  application/schema+json
ok  /spec/did-management/did/delete/0.1  application/schema+json
ok  /spec/acl/grant/0.1                  text/html
ok  /categories                          text/html
ok  /spec/does-not-exist/0.1             application/schema+json -> 404
ok  /specs/does/not/exist.schema.json    application/schema+json -> 404
ok  /spec/does-not-exist/0.1             text/html -> 200
```

## What this PR changes

Documentation only — the infrastructure is already correct.

#181 asserted the opposite of the truth in two places: *"this origin returns 404
for a missing key, so 403 is not in play"*, in both the script header and the
README. That came from my testing with `aws s3api head-object` under my **own
IAM credentials**, which have broader permissions and duly returned 404 — saying
nothing about what the CloudFront principal sees. I then wrote the wrong
conclusion into the code as a justification for leaving the 403 mapping alone.

Both places are corrected, and both now say to verify with `get-bucket-policy`
rather than by probing as yourself, since that false signal is the actual trap.

The README gains a "The bucket policy is part of this" section so anyone
standing this up on another distribution doesn't repeat it.

title: fix(didcomm): the last three device pushes carry the envelope type
body:
#901 fixed the consent-request push and named three sites it had not reached.
This is those three.

Same defect, same binding rule, same silence: the DIDComm message carried the
**task** type where `trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE` is required with the
`TrustTask` in the body. A conformant peer rejects that — and rejects it
*silently*, because "not an envelope" is indistinguishable from "not addressed
to me".

| site | family | what the breakage cost |
|---|---|---|
| `push_granted` | `task-consent/*` | requester waits for its next poll instead of re-submitting at once |
| `maybe_push_step_up` | `auth/step-up/*` | **delegated step-up approvals never reached the device** |
| `maybe_wake_consent_approver` | `consent/*` | a `wake`-routed approver is never roused |

## The one that mattered

`maybe_push_step_up` had been broken the entire time this shipped, and nothing
surfaced it. The reject still carries the `approveRequest` as a relay fallback,
so the ceremony completes by the slow route while the proactive push lands in a
void — delivered, acked, unreadable.

A push whose only failure mode is *latency* is a push nobody notices is dead.

## Protocol family: confirmed, not assumed

`consent/approve-request/0.1` belongs to **`spec/consent/*`** — the conversation
consent family (`request` / `decision` / `revoke` / `list`, all `1.0`) — not to
`spec/task-consent/*`, the per-task RP→wallet family `consent_request.rs` serves.

It does not change the fix. Neither family puts its task type on the DIDComm
envelope, because the envelope belongs to the **binding**, not the task.

## Also in here

`STEP_UP_APPROVE_REQUEST_TYPE` was the DIDComm message type *and* the document
type. It is now only the document type — and `mint_pending_step_up` reads the
constant instead of repeating the literal, so the two cannot drift apart. Its
`#[cfg(feature = "didcomm")]` gate came off with that move: the mint site is not
DIDComm-specific.

**TSP is untouched, deliberately.** It carries the document bytes directly
(`serde_json::to_vec(doc)` → `send_routed`), so the wrapper is a property of the
DIDComm binding, not of the task. Every `ENVELOPE_TYPE` import is `#[cfg]`-gated
to the feature combination that actually sends over DIDComm, so reduced builds
neither break nor carry an unused import.

**No local URI copies** — `trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE` throughout, per
#901's rule.

## Tests

Four new tests, each asserting the **envelope on the message** and the **task
type inside the document** — the shape #901 established when it un-pinned
`a_resubmit_re_asks_nobody`.

They were checked against the *defect*, not just the fix. Reinstating the old
`message_type` on the step-up push fails `delegated_step_up_push_is_an_envelope`:

```
assertion `left == right` failed: the DIDComm message must carry the binding's envelope type
  left: "https://trusttasks.org/spec/auth/step-up/approve-request/0.2"
 right: "https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope"
```

Compiles clean (no errors, no new warnings) at `--no-default-features` and with
each of `didcomm`, `rest`, `tsp`, `didcomm,tsp`, `rest,didcomm,webvh,tsp`.

## Scope

This is the **browser-extension / device peer** half of the envelope work and is
independent of the did-hosting side. The VTA↔DID-hosting switch
(`webvh_didcomm.rs`) is a separate PR, gated on affinidi-webvh-service#155 being
deployed.

## Pre-merge checklist (guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no client code
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — n/a; these pushes are best-effort notifications with a relay/poll fallback, unchanged
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — unchanged; `send_guaranteed` keeps its existing `deliver_by` + idempotency key
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no new wire type; the *document* is unchanged and only its DIDComm framing is corrected to what the binding already specifies
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — unchanged; these paths already log before the send and warn on enqueue failure
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — no mutations; all three sites are post-commit notifications
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none

**Peer note:** approver stacks that (incorrectly) accepted the bare task type
will now receive the envelope. Both fielded stacks — `vta-mobile-core` and the
browser plugin — already unwrap `ENVELOPE_TYPE`, which is why these pushes were
being dropped rather than mishandled.

title: fix(infra): 404 an unknown Type URI instead of returning the site shell
body:
An unknown or mistyped Type URI asked for as a schema returns `/index.html` with
a **200**:

```
/spec/does-not-exist/0.1   Accept: application/schema+json  →  200 text/html
```

§7.2 items 1–2 require a consumer to fetch a schema and validate against it, so
this is a JSON parse error at best and "validated against nothing" at worst —
the silent-failure shape the last several PRs have been removing.

The cause is the distribution's `404 -> /index.html as 200` custom error
response: the conventional SPA catch-all, correct for browsers, wrong for a
schema consumer.

## Two approaches that don't work

**Scoping it to `/specs/*`.** `CustomErrorResponses` is distribution-wide with
no per-cache-behaviour override, so a dedicated cache behaviour can't opt out.
(This was my suggestion when I first raised the bug; it's wrong.)

**Correcting the status on the way out.** I built a viewer-response function for
exactly that, and it never fires for the case that matters — **CloudFront
doesn't run viewer-response functions for responses it generates itself**, and a
custom error page is one. Measured on the live distribution:

| request | result |
|---|---|
| `/` + schema Accept (real origin 200) | **404** — function ran |
| `/spec/does-not-exist/0.1` + schema Accept (custom error page) | **200** — never ran |

`test-function` confirmed the logic was correct; it simply isn't invoked. I
should have checked the invocation semantics before building it rather than
after deploying it. That function is rolled back, deleted, and not in this
change.

## What does work

Remove the mapping and do the SPA fallback in the **viewer-request** function,
where the rule is ours to scope.

The usual "no file extension → SPA route" heuristic fails here, because
`/spec/acl/grant/0.1` ends in what looks like a `.1` extension. So it's
inverted — everything is an SPA route **except** the real asset trees
(`/assets/`, `/specs/`, `/bindings/`) and the root files, which are exactly what
should 404 when absent:

```
schema negotiation rewrite                    (unchanged)
/assets/, /specs/, /bindings/, root files  →  untouched — origin 404s honestly
everything else                            →  /index.html
```

Nothing can be missed, because the SPA is the default. Net effect:
`/spec/does-not-exist/0.1` gives a schema consumer a real **404** and a browser
the SPA, which renders its own not-found.

## Rollout order is enforced, not remembered

The function must be published with the fallback **before** the mapping is
removed — the other way round 404s every client-side route in the gap.
`remove-spa-error-mapping.sh` refuses to run unless the deployed LIVE function
already contains the fallback:

